analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run public health plan on the ACA marketplaces and expands premium subsidies.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 15, 2026 with 2 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to three House committees and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new public health insurance option, the 'Medicare Exchange health plan,' sold alongside private plans on the ACA marketplaces starting in 2028, paying doctors at Medicare rates. It would also remove the income cap on ACA premium subsidies so higher earners qualify, fix the so-called family glitch, add a temporary $30 billion reinsurance fund to lower individual-market premiums, give Medicare direct authority to negotiate Part D drug prices, and fund $150 million a year in health-care antitrust enforcement. It was referred to three House committees and has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying insurance on the individual and small-group marketplaces, who would get a public plan option and no upper income limit on premium subsidies; families squeezed by employer coverage costs through the family-glitch fix; and patients who would benefit from lower drug prices and stronger antitrust enforcement in health-care markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace enrollees and families paying high premiums

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a low-cost public health plan available in every rating area of the individual and small-group markets beginning plan year 2028, sold through the ACA exchanges. [S2]
The plan must cover primary care with no cost-sharing for enrollees. [S2]

It pays providers at Medicare fee-for-service rates, with the option of up to 50 percent higher rates in rural areas, which would let it charge lower premiums than private plans built on commercial rates. [S2]

Doctors enrolled in Medicare or Medicaid would generally have to participate in the public plan, ensuring a broad provider network from day one, with a narrow opt-out for providers who show participation threatens their ability to operate. [S2]

It removes the 400-percent-of-poverty income cap on ACA premium tax credits, sets a sliding scale topping out at 8.5 percent of income, and fixes the family glitch so family members can get subsidies when employer family coverage costs more than 9.5 percent of household income. [S2]

It strikes the statutory 'non-interference' clause that has barred the Secretary of Health and Human Services from directly negotiating Medicare Part D drug prices, and authorizes a $10 billion-per-year reinsurance program for 2028-2030 to pool the costs of the highest-cost patients and lower individual-market premiums. [S2]
It appropriates $150 million a year for fiscal 2027-2031 to the Justice Department's Antitrust Division and the FTC to study and prosecute anticompetitive practices in health-care markets. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a new government competitor paying Medicare rates; drug makers would face direct Medicare price negotiation; hospitals and physicians would be paid Medicare rates instead of higher commercial rates on public-plan patients. Taxpayers fund $2 billion in startup funds, up to $30 billion in reinsurance, the expanded premium tax credits, and $150 million a year in antitrust enforcement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, drug makers, hospitals, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The public plan's premiums must cover its full actuarial and administrative cost, so the plan gets no ongoing federal subsidy and could end up priced close to private plans rather than dramatically cheaper. [S2]

The mandatory provider-participation rule is softened by an opt-out available only in 'exceptional circumstances' where participation threatens a provider's ability to operate, a standard that could invite disputes and network gaps if many providers seek to stay out. [S2]

The reinsurance program is a temporary subsidy to the private individual market (authorized only for 2028-2030) rather than a permanent cost fix, and removing the 400-percent income cap on premium tax credits adds open-ended federal spending with no offset in the bill. [S2]
The bill does not change Medicare benefits or trust funds and does not extend the public plan to the large-group market, so its reach is limited to the individual and small-group markets. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For marketplace shoppers, the bill bundles real gains: a cheaper public option, no subsidy cliff at 400 percent of poverty, a family-glitch fix, free primary care, and an anti-monopoly enforcement fund. The costs are real but conventional: taxpayer-funded start-up and reinsurance money, open-ended subsidy expansion without offsets, and lower payments flowing to insurers, drug makers, and providers. The design is more incremental than a Medicare-for-all approach, but the mandatory provider participation and Medicare-rate payment would make the public plan a serious competitor rather than a token option.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 15, 2026 and sent to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — and none of them has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced H.R. 9702 on July 15, 2026, joined by Reps. Norton and Quigley. [S2]
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committees on Ways and Means and Judiciary. [S4]
The cosponsor count stands at 2 House Democrats. [S3]
The full action history shows no further steps: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action has been recorded since the July 15 referral. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the outcome is a stalemate rather than a defeat: nothing has been decided. If the bill dies in committee when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, the winners will be the private insurers, drug makers, and providers who would have faced a Medicare-rate public competitor and direct drug-price negotiation — ordinary marketplace enrollees will have gained nothing. Nothing in the record so far changes anyone's position, but time is running out for this Congress to act on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; insurers benefit if it dies

sides.party_line_note: The only support in the record is Democratic — a Democratic sponsor and 2 Democratic cosponsors out of 217 House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors — and all three committees holding the bill have Republican chairs.

industries.note: A public plan paying Medicare rates would compete directly with private marketplace plans in the individual and small-group markets, drawing customers with lower premiums. The bill's $10 billion-a-year temporary reinsurance fund softens the blow by subsidizing premiums across the private individual market. [S2]

The bill repeals the 'non-interference' clause that has barred HHS from directly negotiating Part D drug prices, and the public plan would pay rates negotiated by the Secretary. Drug makers have an interest in keeping direct negotiation off the table, which would otherwise lower what patients and taxpayers pay. [S2]

Providers treating public-plan patients would be paid Medicare rates, generally below commercial insurance rates, and Medicare/Medicaid-enrolled providers would generally be required to participate. The bill offers an offset: up to 50 percent higher reimbursement in rural areas, which could strengthen rural hospitals' finances. [S2]

The Secretary is authorized to contract out administrative functions for the new plan the same way Medicare does, creating administrative business for existing claims-processing contractors, though the contract cannot shift insurance risk off the government. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: The bill is on the standard path to quietly expiring: referred to three committees in July 2026, with no hearings, markups, or votes since, and only 2 cosponsors in a chamber where major health legislation rarely reaches the floor without committee action. It would need committee approval in at least one committee and a floor vote before January 3, 2027 — without new cosponsors or leadership interest, it is almost certain to die when this Congress ends.
